pages.x: Carthage had built an empire in southern Spain, rich in silver, and from there Hannibal set out in 218 BC to invade Italy. To cut him off from his base, Rome landed an army in the north-east, at the Greek port of Emporion. Spain became the second front of the war.

Both Roman commanders, the Scipio brothers, were killed in 211 BC. The son of one of them, the young Publius Scipio, took over, and in 209 BC stormed New Carthage, the enemy's capital in Spain, sending men across a lagoon as the water fell. At Ilipa in 206 BC he drove the Carthaginians out of Spain.

Rome stayed. In 197 BC it made the coasts into two provinces, and governors came to collect tribute, often with a heavy hand. The peoples of the interior, the Celtiberians of the hills and the Lusitanians of the west, rose again and again. Cato, sent to crush them, boasted that he had taken more towns in Spain than he had spent days there.

In 150 BC a governor massacred thousands of Lusitanians who had laid down their arms. One who escaped, a shepherd named Viriathus, led eight years of guerrilla war from the hills, beating army after army. In 139 BC Rome bribed three of his friends to murder him in his sleep; when they asked for their reward, the story goes, they were told that Rome does not pay traitors.

The hill town of Numantia defied Rome for ten years. In 134 BC Scipio Aemilianus, who had destroyed Carthage, ringed it with walls and camps nine kilometres long, and starved it. When it fell, many Numantines killed themselves rather than surrender, and the town was razed.

In the 70s BC Spain became a battlefield of Rome's own civil wars. Quintus Sertorius, a Roman rebel, won the Lusitanians and Celtiberians to his side, kept a white fawn that he said brought him messages from the goddess Diana, and beat the Senate's armies, the young Pompey's among them, until his own officers murdered him at dinner in 72 BC.

Only the mountains of the north still held out. In 26 BC the emperor Augustus came in person to fight the Cantabrians and Astures, who, the Romans said, would rather die than be enslaved. Revolts flared until his general Agrippa ended them in 19 BC, two centuries after the Romans first landed.

Hispania became one of the most Roman parts of the empire. It gave Rome the emperors Trajan and Hadrian, the writer Seneca, silver and olive oil, and its Latin grew into Spanish, Portuguese and Catalan. Roman bridges, aqueducts and theatres still stand across Spain and Portugal.

Two centuries of war for the interior
Its Latin grew into Spanish and Portuguese
